NEWBORN INTENSIVE CARE

By: Tarryn Crossman | Paid

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Larissa and her husband only touched their son Hayden for the first time 46 days after he was born, and a few hours before he passed away.
For 46 days their pleas for KMC or to just touch their child fell on deaf ears, as day after day they were told: “it's hospital protocol to keep covid out of the NICU”.
Hayden did eventually get Covid, from a doctor in the ward. He was in 14 days of isolation when he had to under an emergency bowel operation, his doctor knew that he may never make it through surgery, but hospital policy forbids his parents from seeing him at all prior to the operation.
After 5 days of threatening legal action, Larissa and her husband were finally allowed to see their extremely ill son through a piece of class. “The nurse held him up like Simba, I could see that he was in distress from being held up and told her to please put him down. It was more distressing than not seeing him at all”


Marissa was only allowed to visit her son twice a day and only one parent per day was permitted. She arrived at Sunninghill NICU one day to find her son under a blanket, which she thought was strange. But nothing could have prepared her for when she removed the heavy blanket. Her 1.5kg son’s arms had been tapped to his diaper. According to the doctor she did it to put in an IV line and told the nurses to remove it when she was done. According to the nurses, they forgot, and due to covid restrictions Marissa was only able to visit for 15 minutes3 times a day, so that tape had been holding her son down for hours

“Anna” was rushed in for an emergency C-section, and her baby girl was airlifted to a Netcare hospital (still trying to get her to tell me which one) 2 hours from their home. She lived there for 8 weeks, anna was only allowed to visit for one hour a day and her husband (baby girl's father) was only permitted on a Sunday for 30 minutes. Her baby girl died without Anna ever touching her.

These are just some of the parents that will live with the trauma of not being able to hold or comfort their babies, for the rest of their lives.

In an open letter to Life, Netcare, and Mediclinic over 400 parents addressed their concerns with the management of the private nicus during the pandemic. The rules seemed to be random and not based on science. The British Association of Perinatal Medicine states that ‘’it is essential that the mother and her partner are never considered to be visitors within the neonatal unit – they are partners in their baby’s care and their presence should be encouraged and facilitated as much as possible.’’ Additionally, the guidance encourages services to reflect on how best to maximize involvement and facilitate parental presence at all times – including during ward rounds - while maintaining social distancing, and sets out that parents should be supported to be involved and present during end-of-life care, even if COVID-19 positive.


According to a study done by WHO in March 2021, they found that
“Disruptions to essential health services during COVID-19 have severely affected the quality of care provided to some of the most vulnerable babies, and this includes their right to the lifesaving contact they need with their parents,” said Dr. Anshu Banerjee, Director for Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and Ageing at WHO.

In WHO’s study, they found the removal of Kangaroo care from NICU units life-threatening, Kangaroo’ing has been proven to reduce infant deaths by as much as 40%, hypothermia by more than 70%, and severe infections by 65%.

Pretorius
But according to NICU nursing expert Linda Pretorius, these issues in the level of care being offered in private NICU units is not just a COVID problem. “There is a complete lack of understanding about the developmental needs of these prem babies and the long-term damage that their NICU stay will have on their lives if they live”

She highlighted issues with the lighting in the units, the loud noises, no kangaroo care, which she is mainly due to laziness from nurses and doctors and a general lack of understanding and care from nurses with regards to the long-term neurodevelopment of these babies.
“The removal of the parent has been devastating, if these babies survive they will have severe emotional and physical side effects due to a lack of bonding within their first 1000 days and the level of trauma being left alone in the NICU has caused them.”

I tell the nurses I teach over and over “You know the baby is dying let them hold their blady child!”

Prod Shabir Mahdi has also weighed in on the issue. On Twitter, he responded to Marissa’s taped-down baby by saying that “mother and newborn bonding is critical and cannot be recovered sometime in the future. Need to manage the risk factors…
He would be a good expert

Script:


After 3 years, we’re emerging from a pandemic, trying to make sense of the global response to a virus we now know much more about. Were the regulations governing our lives necessary, or - with hindsight – were some too extreme?

we mustn't underestimate how difficult these decisions were because we were in a situation of the unknown, and the fear factor was very high. about COVID transmission.

To protects, patients and staff from infection, hospitals in many parts of the world either closed their doors to visitors or enforced strict admission rules. At many of our private neonatal intensive care units, babies were separated from their parents at birth, robbing them of early attachment, with possible serious long-term effects.

Professor Haroon Saloojee, head of Community Paediatrics at Wits University, was active in the COVID protocols debates.

the guidance is clear. Newborns should have 24-hour access, so there's no doubt about that, that the deficit for mothers not being present during COVID will and will have consequences for the children.

Larissa and Marlon Scholtz were told their first child, who they’d named Hayden, would be 3 months premature. He was born in mid-June last year, weighing just 500 grams, and was immediately admitted to the Neonatal Intensive care unit or NICU at Joburg’s Netcare Park Lane.

we knew that he would be a low birth weight and a microchip. And that wasn't going to be an easy road.

What they didn’t know is how limited their access would be to their son. In July, as COVID numbers soared during the 3rd wave, the Netcare hospital group limited visitation to the NICU to one parent per day for no longer than 2-3 hours.

The protocols and the regulations imposed by the hospital itself prevented both parents from seeing your child. So we got one visit when he was still in the hospital to go together. The last time we stood together was... when he passed.

Before Hayden died, Larissa and Marlon went through daily covid screenings and had to wear gloves, masks, visors, and aprons before being allowed into the NICU to see him.

We never got to touch him with our skin, with gloves on. And with all those protocols in place, Hayden contracted COVID-19 anyway. Did they tell you how? No one wanted to tell us who it was, and they insinuated that it could have been us and asked us to go get tested. And when we got tested, we found out that we were negative, But they already had their suspicions. Who could have been from within?
The surgeon called to say. That You need to just the babies that I was working with. They knew it was him.

Netcare says, “Medical information of a third party is privileged”, and so they couldn’t inform the parents about the likely source of the infection.

Hayden was placed in isolation days before major bowel surgery, and despite his doctor requesting that the parents be allowed to see him, the hospital declined.

We practically begged, and they said no. But his doctor video called us before they gave him anesthetic, and we saw him on a video call.

In their response to us, Netcare reiterate that baby Hayden had tested positive for COVID-19, and both the parents and the baby were required to isolate.



After three rounds of fertility treatment, Marissa Terblanche, who is hearing impaired, fell pregnant with miracle twins. Due to complications, they were delivered in early May last year at just 26 weeks. The babies were immediately admitted to the NICU at Jo’burg’s Mediclinic Midstream.

It was my first experience with NICU, everybody is walking slowly and speaking softly, it was very peaceful and calm.

After two weeks, Marissa’s son Kayden needed heart surgery, so he was transferred to the NICU at Netcare Sunninghill.

I remember I was really shocked. It was very, very loud. It was always very uncomfortable being there.
I don't think THEY KNOW how to be compassionate.

Not only were the environments at the two private NICUs different, they also had completely different covid rules and regulations.

At mediclinic you were allowed at all times. I visited there the whole day, but I was allowed to, you know, come and go as I pleased They even offered me so I can take my laptop work and work from there. And at Sunninghill, they only allowed one parent at a time for one hour.

This lack of consistency was evident in both state and private NICU, which begs the question: how much of the response was based on science?

The South African Paediatric Association tried to promote the idea that caregivers should have more access. But in the end, the decision is left to individual clinics or individual hospitals. So there were no guidelines On this specific issue. That kind of guidance didn't come through from the National Department of Health because it was such a difficult decision and a lot of it is context-dependent.

Devastated at being separated from their babies, over 400 parents signed this open letter last year questioning the science behind the Covid regulations applied at NICU's at all private hospital groups. They argued for more access.

00:53:55:02 - 00:54:00:23
It's not something that any parent should have to go through.

Dr Dr Ida Du Plessis-Fauri worked as a neonatal nurse for over 20 years. She’s now a consultant.

the neonatal ICU is supposed to provide an environment that mimics the womb. That means that baby must be able to hear the mother He knows her voice. He also has to smell the parents Then, The baby can self-regulate He doesn't go into stress mode. Remember, when a baby's in a stress mode,
the blood supply will go to the brain, the heart, and the lungs. And there's a shortage of blood supply in the intestines, kidneys, and everywhere else. And that can cause long-term effects
for the baby.

MARISSA:
I remember when I went to stroke his head, they said, “leave him alone.” They always hide behind the excuse “It’s not good for the baby”, but we both know they need touch?

At Netcare Sunninghill, Marissa wasn’t allowed to touch Kayden at all. According to the Netcare group, this was due to the Covid restrictions, as well as his critical condition. At Mediclinic Midstream, though, nurses insisted she hold her daughter daily even though she was also critical and would eventually pass away.

almost every day I sat there they were always very willing, The machine didn't care about the pipes. Always no need to disconnect the pipes and everything. But, you had to move the automated fence

to clean it up. But yeah, they always were willing to pass it on. They moved their machines closer to the issue with that because they see the benefit in holding a baby.

How important is touch for babies.

Absolutely critical. What has now been globally accepted is something called skin to skin care. It's a concept now over 30 years and the whole idea is that for these very small babies, the ideal way to manage them is soon after they are born You put them on to the mother's chest and you do that for the full 24 hours.

The benefits of skin to skin or kangaroo maternal care, for even just an hour a day, are profound. Studies say it reduces infant deaths by as much as 40%, hypothermia by 70% and sever infection by 65%.

00:24:31:09 - 00:25:05:22
There's been comparisons of babies who had this exposure to mums and babies who haven't. And there's so many domains that that the improvement happened by reducing baby stress, all these physiological variables such as heart rate and despite rate immediately go down. And if you can control that, there's a better chance that you'll get babies out of ICU earlier,
00:25:05:24 - 00:25:27:07
mothers who talk to the babies, touch their babies, that kind of sensory stimulation is vital for baby's
Initially for reassurance that I'm a human being, they recognize their mothers, but subsequently there's enough evidence that those babies outcome longer term, we're talking about two or three
even going to school going age, are much better than when they haven't had that kind of interaction.

In their response to us, Netcare explained Kangaroo Care as a therapeutic regime used in under resourced environments. Historically, Netcare did offer a modified version of KMC in the NICU but it was temporarily discontinued during the pandemic.

public hospitals have embraced the concept My disappointment is that the private sector, private clinics haven't embraced it in the same way. And there's no reason to believe that kangaroo mother case for poor or uneducated or backward mothers, that perception is absolutely wrong.

Some NICU’s, like the one here at Sebokeng Hospital, near Vereeniging, never closed their doors; they consider parents primary caregivers rather than visitors. This hospital’s 24-hour KMC unit was also operational throughout COVID.

Here at the neonatal intensive care unit at the hospital. It's both heart-breaking and incredible to see mothers being able to care for the critically ill babies, because that's all that,. Larissa and Morris ever wanted, just to touch their babies

In March last year, months before any of these babies being admitted to the NICU, the World Health Organisation published a study advising hospitals to keep mother and child together, encouraging skin-on-skin care during the PANDEMIC.

LINK: cover the front of this?
Parents understood the need for the regulations around COVID-19, especially when it was new and when there was extreme panic. But as the different waves progressed and we learned more, more and more studies found that the benefits of KMC far outweigh the health risks of COVID-19. Yet these policies didn't keep up

00:03:44:24 - 00:04:28:14
I think the criticism
would be that we perhaps prevailed for too long with policies that were initially established, and we should have been much quicker in increasing access to these young infants to their parents.

Hayden survived his surgery, and on day 5 of his quarantine, the hospital finally agreed to allow his parents to see him.

We got a call from management to say that. They've arranged for 5 minutes.
When we got there, it was still a guy in full PPE and using an isolation unit at the time. So the nurse held him up. We looked at him through a. Window, So the plan was for the nurse to hold Hayden. And for you to look at him while he's being held up.

With such limited access, parents could not be a part of the day-to-day management of their babies, having instead to trust the nursing staff. Arriving at Netcare Sunninghill in late June last year, Marissa was horrified to find her 1.7kg son’s hands placed inside his nappy and taped to his body.

We asked the nurse, what is happening here? And she didn't answer me, she just called another nurse.

According to Netcare, Kayden was mildly sedated and then restrained so that his treating doctor could insert a central line. The treating doctor was clear this is standard protocol because of the danger of an infant moving during the procedure.

So I have never in my life have I seen this, not once in my life and as qualified in 1994. It's appalling.

Netcare explain that Kayden was still retrained as staff were waiting for an x-ray confirming the correct placement of the central line. Marissa recalls Kayden being alert when the nurse finally removed the tape.

I remember him screaming and screaming, and I just wanted to pick him up, but I'm not allowed.

After Hayden's 10-day isolation, Larissa was allowed to see her son, but his health had radically deteriorated.

the nurses even said you know what? All you can do at this point is put.

On the day that Hayden died, Netcare allowed both parents into the unit and suggested they try and hold their son.

He was sick We just didn't want him to be disturbed. We only touched his hands
when he passed away. So you never. Got to feel his flesh and Blood? No, it was cold.

Beat

NETCARE says Hayden wasn’t medically stable enough to be held or touched prior to the day he died. But they did say, “Looking at events now with the benefit of hindsight, we feel that greater parental access could have been possible.”

I don't think it's acceptable. I could never argue that the risk of infection or infecting everybody else was so high that that situation could not be controlled. That's just inhumane.

Hayden lived for 43 days; he never got to smell or touch his mother; beyond the constant medical procedures, he had no meaningful physical contact with another human being.

You know, at the end of the day, I gave birth physically to Haydon I have a scar to prove that he's ours, but really, truly wasn't ours

Five days after finding him restrained, Marissa had Kayden returned to Mediclinic Midstream, and a few weeks later, he was discharged. He’s now over a year old.
